actuation: rotatory DC motor (DJI RoboMaster M3508 P19) with actuating tendon
constitutive_assumptions: Soft material is incompressible and homogeneous
No strain exists in the tendon (inextensible tendon)
Strain only lies in the junction zone, while other regions are rigid enough without any deformation (stress concentration assumption)
The spring during bending is approximated as an arc shape
Spring length is constant under pretension force, but undergoes length variation along with joint bending when pretension force is removed
Deformation is modeled as a quasi-static process
Angle variation of each joint is assumed to be equal under small displacement at the fingertip (alpha1 = alpha2)
control_variables: Finger dimensions and structural geometry (junction zone parameters a, b, c, and tendon distance)
Hyperelastic material coefficients for Agilus 30 (C1 = 0.168, C2 = 0.023) and junction zone expansion factor (mu = 2)
Number of repeated experimental trials per condition (3 repetitions averaged)
Initial contact force before dynamic oscillation (set to 0.5 N)
Displacement testing increment for stiffness characterization (1 mm interval up to 8 mm)
dependent_variables: Bending moment (actuating moment, resistance moment, and spring rotational moment)
Horizontal pulling resistance force / load capacity (N)
Deformation or structural damage of fragile objects (paper ring, plasticine cylinder, paper cup)
Dynamic grasp stability and contact force oscillation during periodic reciprocal motion

evidence_relevant_to_topic.claim: Combining spring stiffness and pretension under the antagonistic mechanism can enhance fingertip stiffness up to 6.4 times compared to a finger without springs.
The joint bending deformation and resistance moment can be modeled using second-order Yeoh hyperelastic strain energy density combined with a stress-concentration sector geometry.
Finger stiffness can be predicted via virtual work and equivalent series joint stiffness, showing positive correlation with spring pretension and bending angle.
Selective spring pretensioning allows single-joint bending where the stiffened joint remains unbent while the compliant joint bends up to 70 degrees under load.

A stiffness gradient decreasing from base to tip produces sequential motion (proximal sweeping followed by distal caging) that enlarges contact area and reduces mismatching zones across various cylinder curvatures.
Increasing spring pretension and wire diameter decreases normal clamping force because the antagonistic effect offsets bending torque, enabling gentle contact.
Stiffening the distal joint is more effective at strengthening lateral load capacity than stiffening the proximal joint.
Variable joint stiffness protects delicate objects, allowing undamaged grasping of paper rings and plasticine cylinders that deform or fail under uniform stiffness.

Antagonistic pretensioning enables stable dynamic grasping of a 100 g weighted paper cup under reciprocal motion (1.4 s cycle) without slip, whereas fingers without pretension bend passively and fail due to inertial forces.

experimental_setup: Multimaterial 3D printing of fingers using PolyJet 750 (Stratasys Inc.) with Vero PureWhite for rigid backbones and Agilus 30 for soft attachments
Actuation test rig using a rotatory DC motor (DJI RoboMaster M3508 P19) for the actuating tendon and two servomotors (TianKongRC TD-8320MG) for antagonist spring tendons
Deformation measurement platform with finger mounted on a 3D-printed holder and positions tracked on grid paper under 300 g and 500 g hanging weights
Stiffness testing platform using a force meter (SF-200, Aipu) mounted on a linear screw guide pushing the fingertip horizontally by 8 mm in 1 mm increments

Clamping force and load capacity station using a flexible force sensor (FlexiForce A201, Tekscan Inc.) attached to the distal phalange and pulling force measured axially and laterally during object escape
Dynamic manipulation setup with SRSG mounted on a robotic manipulator performing reciprocal motion with a 1.4 s period while holding a paper cup containing 100 g weight

Grasping verification across diverse shapes: cylinders (35, 45, 55, 60, 75 mm), cuboids (50, 80 mm), triangular prism, paper cups with weights (100 g, 200 g), 1 kg weight, 410 mL drink, paper ring, and plasticine cylinder
independent_variables: Spring wire diameter (e.g., 0.6 mm vs. other diameters / without springs)
Spring pretension force and elongation length (0 to 8 mm; up to 2.9 N)
Actuating tendon force / applied hanging weight (e.g., 300 g, 500 g, up to 9.7 N)
Joint bending angle (e.g., 10 deg, 20 deg, up to 70 deg or 90 deg)
Joint stiffness configuration/gradient (uniform, base-to-tip decreasing, proximal stiffened)
Target object geometry, dimension, and deformability (curvatures of 35-75 mm, flat cuboids, triangular shape, fragile/compliant items)
Dynamic oscillation state (reciprocal manipulator motion with 1.4 s period)
limitations_inferred: Multi-material 3D-printed elastomer-to-rigid interfaces (Agilus 30 to Vero PureWhite) may be vulnerable to fatigue and delamination under repetitive antagonistic loading.
The variable stiffness mechanism relies on pre-programmed open-loop servo positions without real-time closed-loop contact force or stiffness sensing.
Each finger is mechanically constrained to single-plane bending without lateral adduction/abduction or spatial compliance.
External actuators (DC motor, multiple servos, and controller) add system bulk, limiting self-contained untethered deployment.
limitations_stated_by_authors: Discrepancies and errors exist between theoretical modeling predictions and experimental results due to nonlinear material behavior and approximate mathematical solutions.
The gripper without spring pretension suffers from insufficient stiffness to resist inertial forces during dynamic acceleration and deceleration, causing passive bending and grasp failure.
main_results: The finger stiffness increased up to 6.4-fold when combining spring stiffness and pretension compared to the finger without springs.
Applying spring pretension up to 2.9 N increased finger stiffness from 0.223 to 0.425 N/mm at a 20-degree joint angle.

Stiffness gradient allocation enabled sequential motion (proximal bending sweeping followed by distal caging), significantly enlarging contact area across various object curvatures (35, 55, and 75 mm diameters).
Higher distal joint stiffness contributed more significantly to lateral load capacity than proximal joint stiffness.
Antagonistic pretensioning reduced peak contact clamping force while elevating structural resistance, allowing gentle and safe grasping of fragile paper rings and plasticine cylinders without damage.

The gripper lifted heavy items (1 kg weights, 410 mL drink) and maintained dynamic grasp stability on a 100 g weighted paper cup over four 1.4 s reciprocal cycles without slipping, whereas fingers without pretension dropped the object.
modeling_methods: Moment equilibrium modeling considering actuating moment, joint hyperelastic resistance moment, and spring rotational moment
Stress concentration modeling idealizing the deformed junction zone as a sector of bending angle theta with expansion factor mu = 2
Second-order Yeoh hyperelastic strain energy density formulation for incompressible, homogeneous soft material
Virtual work principle formulating joint reaction torque and stiffness from total strain and potential energy
Series equivalent stiffness model for two independent joints in series (Kf = K1*K2 / (K1 + K2))
performance_metrics: Finger stiffness (N/mm) and stiffness enhancement ratio (up to 6.4x)
Maximum joint bending angle (up to 90 degrees per joint)
Horizontal pulling resistance force / axial load capacity (N)
Contact area and surface conformity (reduction of mismatching interaction zone)
Preservation of fragile object geometry without deformation/damage
Dynamic grip retention under reciprocal motion cycles (1.4 s period)
possible_gap_implications: Although the antagonistic tendon-spring mechanism avoids the bulky fluidic hardware of pneumatic variable-stiffness grippers, achieving autonomous stiffness adaptation in unstructured environments will likely require integrating tactile/proprioceptive feedback.
While sequential planar motion improves curvature enveloping, grasping highly irregular three-dimensional or asymmetric objects with antagonistic variable stiffness remains an open research avenue.
The durability, creep, and fatigue life of multimaterial 3D-printed joints subjected to continuous antagonistic pretension warrant systematic cyclic endurance testing.
paper.research_objective: To develop, model, and experimentally validate a bioinspired soft-rigid structured gripper (SRSG) utilizing an antagonistic tendon-spring mechanism to achieve variable joint stiffness, sequential motion, and mutable postures for conformal, safe, and stable grasping of delicate and varied objects.
paper.research_problem: Conventional soft grippers struggle to reconcile high compliance with variable stiffness for delicate and high-load tasks, while existing variable stiffness mechanisms often suffer from poor repeatability, slow response, or complex control; furthermore, uniform curvature deformation limits adaptability to diverse curvatures and risks damaging fragile items.
stiffness_mechanism: multimaterial soft joint with spring connecting adjacent backbones
paper.title: A Bioinspired Gripper with Sequential Motion and Mutable Posture Enabled by Antagonistic Mechanism
